The inquiry into the Northgate warehouse fire opened on a damp Tuesday morning, and by nine the hearing room was full. Counsel for the county began by reading the timeline aloud, pausing at each entry as though the dates themselves might explain what six inspections had missed. The building had stood on the eastern edge of the industrial estate since the early nineteen eighties, and in that time it had changed hands five times, each sale recorded in a ledger that the clerk now placed before the panel.

Witnesses described a routine that had gone unexamined for years. Forklift operators worked in rotating shifts, stacking pallets of paper, paint and cleaning fluid in rows that crept closer to the heating ducts as the seasons passed. A former supervisor, speaking quietly and often looking at her hands, said that nobody had ever been asked to measure the gap between the stacks and the wall. The company's safety officer agreed that the written guidance was vague, though he insisted the practice had been consistent with the standards then in force. He was asked, more than once, who exactly had signed off on the latest risk assessment. Each time he named a different manager.

The panel then heard from residents of the streets beyond the estate. Several described smoke drifting low over the rooftops and ash settling on washing left out overnight. One woman recalled banging on doors as the sirens started. Another said the alarm had rung for years, usually on windy nights, so that most people had stopped paying attention. An electrician who had serviced the site in the spring told the hearing that the panel controlling the sprinkler pumps had been bypassed sometime before Christmas, and that he had reported this in writing. His report, the panel noted, had never been answered.

After lunch the inquiry turned to the night of the fire itself. A delivery driver testified that he had parked his van outside the loading bay and walked toward the security cabin, where the lights were off and a radio still murmured on the windowsill. He remembered a smell like burning rubber and a sound he could only describe as a low roar. Within minutes, he said, the shutter at the far end of the loading bay had begun to glow. Fire crews arrived from the station on Mill Road in under six minutes, but by then the smoke had already forced them back from the main doors.

An expert in structural fire behaviour was asked whether the collapse could have been predicted. She explained, patiently and at length, that warehouses of this age often concealed voids above the false ceilings, and that fires in such voids tend to travel sideways before they are noticed. The building had no internal compartmentation to speak of, she added, and the roof materials had degraded faster than the drawings suggested. When pressed, she declined to say that a single inspection would have prevented the collapse.

The hearing continues tomorrow, when the panel is expected to hear evidence from the owners and from the contractor responsible for maintenance. Counsel for the families has indicated that she will ask why the sprinkler system remained offline for the better part of a year, and who, if anyone, was monitoring the alarms that so many neighbours had learned to ignore.
